Empirical Research Plan – Police Size and Crime  

─────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two–stage least squares (panel IV) with city and year fixed effects, using the mayoral-election cycle as an instrument for police force size.  
Why IV?  
• Endogenous police staffing (cities hire more officers when crime rises).  
• Mayoral elections create plausibly exogenous, discrete bumps in hiring that are not mechanically tied to contemporaneous crime shocks.  
• Annual panel of >10 years and >200 cities gives power for FE-IV.  
Complementary diagnostics: event-study graph of police staffing around elections to show pre-trends and dynamic treatment profile.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment (endogenous variable): Police force size, measured as officers per 1,000 residents (PoliceRate_ct).  
Instrument (Z_ct): ElectionYear_ct = 1 if city c holds a regularly scheduled mayoral election in year t, 0 otherwise.  
Control (counterfactual): Same city in non-election years; other cities whose election calendars are in off-cycle years. With city FE, each city serves as its own control.  
Timing: ElectionYear takes the value 1 in calendar year t of the election; robustness check re-defines as t–1 (budgeting year) and t+1 (post-election) to verify timing.  
No running variable is used; not an RDD.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Relevance – ElectionYear significantly increases PoliceRate. Plausible: campaign incentives to “hire cops”. Can be tested (first-stage F-stat > 10).  
A2. Exclusion – Conditional on city & year FE and controls, ElectionYear affects crime only through PoliceRate (no direct or alternative channels). Plausibility: other public-safety policies that coincide with elections are limited; will add controls for policing budget, public-works spending, and state/federal transfers.  
A3. Parallel trends / no differential anticipation – Crime trends in pre-election years are parallel to non-election years. Checked via event-study coefficients for t–3…t–1.  
A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) – No cross-city spillovers in crime attributable to election-driven hiring (checked by adding neighboring-city election dummies).  
A5. Monotonicity – Election years do not reduce police staffing in any city (supported by descriptive stats).

4. Main Threats & Mitigation  
T1. Simultaneous “tough-on-crime” policies (e.g., sentencing changes) adopted in election years.  
 • Mitigation: control for city-level law-and-order ordinances, policing budget shares, and state sentencing reforms (state×year FE).  
T2. Crime reporting or clearance manipulation by police in election years (pressure to look good).  
 • Mitigation: focus on 911 calls (where available) and homicide (hard to under-report); run results separately for reported vs. victimization survey data in subset of cities.  
T3. Endogenous election timing (special elections after scandals/crime waves).  
 • Mitigation: restrict instrument to regularly-scheduled elections; drop special elections; instrument strength unaffected.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ----------------- 0. Packages -----------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast FE-IV
library(ggplot2)

# ----------------- 1. Load ---------------------
ucr <- fread("ucr_city_year.csv")   # assume variables: city_id, year, pop, officers, violent, property, election

# ----------------- 2. Construct ----------------
ucr[, PoliceRate := (officers / pop) * 1000]
ucr[, ViolentRate := (violent / pop) * 100000]
ucr[, PropRate    := (property / pop) * 100000]

# Instrument
ucr[, ElectionYear := election]   # 1 if reg. mayoral election

# Controls
ucr[, UnempRate := unemployed / labor_force]  # example
ucr[, Income_pc := income / pop]

# ----------------- 3. First Stage --------------
fs <- feols(PoliceRate ~ ElectionYear + UnempRate + Income_pc | city_id + year,
            data = ucr, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(fs)

# ----------------- 4. Second Stage -------------
iv <- feols(ViolentRate ~ UnempRate + Income_pc | city_id + year | 
            PoliceRate ~ ElectionYear, data = ucr, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(iv)

# ----------------- 5. Event-Study --------------
ucr[, rel_year := year - election_year_actual] # needs actual election year var
est <- feols(PoliceRate ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1) | city_id + year,
             data = ucr[abs(rel_year)<=4], cluster = ~city_id)
iplot(est)

# ----------------- 6. Robustness: Placebo ------
ucr[, PostElection := (year == election_year_actual + 2)]
placebo <- feols(ViolentRate ~ UnempRate + Income_pc | city_id + year | 
                 PoliceRate ~ PostElection, data = ucr, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(placebo)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory (deterrence/incapacitation) predicts a negative elasticity: more officers → lower crime. Prior literature suggests −0.10 to −0.20 elasticity for violent crime. With mean violent crime ≈ 600 per 100k, adding 1 officer per 1,000 residents (≈ +12 %) may lower violent crime by 6–12 % (≈ 36–72 crimes per 100k).

7. Validity Checklist (IV) – Self-Assessment  
C1. Instrument relevance ………………… 1  
C2. Exclusion restriction ………………… 0.5 (some direct election effects possible)  
C3. No endogenous sample selection …… 1  
C4. Monotonicity / no defiers …………… 1  
C5. Stable relationships over time ……… 0.5 (crime technology may change)  
Total: 4 / 5

─────────────────────────────────────────────
This plan exploits politically driven, plausibly exogenous swings in police staffing to identify the causal impact of officers on crime, while addressing major empirical threats with fixed effects, rich controls, event-study diagnostics, and robustness exercises.
